rewrites.summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

The consequence axis reaches custody: under the Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act (2026) transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons based on sex assigned at birth, and since April 2024 state law has banned gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates — so a trans visitor arrested here is housed by birth sex with no gender-affirming care allowed behind the walls.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent litigation and policy flux: the Supreme Court upheld the state's ban on gender-affirming care for minors in June 2025, and the drag ban's constitutionality has never been decided on the merits. A civil-liberties suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event also remains ongoing.

The Riley Gaines Act's adjacent provision also bars trans women from women's shelters — a facility restriction beyond prisons attached to the same 2026 statute.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters — a resident-facing facility practice.

The April 2024 in-prison ban on gender-affirming care governs the treatment of residents held in state custody.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No drag-ban prosecutions are publicly reported, so actual charging practice is unverified. The killing-rate figure rests on 10 recorded deaths (2008–2025), treated as an undercount floor.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement mandate is statutory (2026), but no Tennessee case, ruling, special unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented; the prison and shelter provisions come from a single Wikipedia state-rights article, the only prison-axis source in this record.

rewrites.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

The consequence axis reaches custody on two fronts: the Women's Privacy Act expressly applies to prisons and other state government buildings — but on restroom use matching the sex on one's birth certificate, not on cell or facility assignment — while in Gibson v. Collier (2019) the Texas prison system denied a transgender inmate gender-confirmation surgery under its official policy, and the courts affirmed no deliberate indifference, treating the refusal as a permissible medical choice, leaving a trans person in Texas custody without a proven judicial remedy for denial of gender-affirming care.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
LGB-facing visibility is rolling back too: Arlington's city council rescinded its LGBTQ non-discrimination ordinance (Dec 2025) and Arlington Pride suspended its 2026 events; a Houston-area venue pulled out of Katy Pride under school-board pressure.

Litigation flux: in Gibson v. Collier (2019) a federal court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against the transgender inmate on the Eighth Amendment claim, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed the dismissal (with a dissenting opinion on summary-judgement procedure) — documentation of Texas' denial practice more than a change in it.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Document governance is resident-facing but nationally anomalous: DPS has ignored court-ordered gender-marker changes and built a database of applicants seeking them.

The denial practice is resident-facing: Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman incarcerated with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the department's official treatment policy excluded it.

Collier is a treatment case, not a placement ruling.

rewrites.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban — the nation's current ruling movement — is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. A 2024 Morality Law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; the ruling movement applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that international experts say is escalating into 2026. The prison-housing axis is thin but must not read as neutral: nothing is documented on where trans prisoners are held — no birth-sex vs identity housing rule, no trans special units, no solitary or segregation practice — while Human Rights Watch / OutRight International (January 2022, 60 interviews) documents wrongful-detention risk, threats, assault and blackmail of LGBTI people since the takeover; in a criminalising regime with no recourse, an undocumented placement practice means a detained trans visitor is held at the regime's discretion amid the documented abuse of queer detainees, not under any protected standard.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The applicable legal regime is layered and shifting: penal-code "sodomy" provisions carry up to two years, while a Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity and the 2024 Morality Law added surveillance duties; flogging documented by international experts nearly doubled in 2025 to at least 1,110 people.

Asylum-framework context: international guidance treats LGBTIQ people in the country as those perceived to transgress religious and social norms, and refugee-led organisations abroad document systematic persecution — context for the regime's treatment, not visitor-facing advice.

Enforcement context: the Human Rights Watch / OutRight International report (26 January 2022) records Taliban members using leaked personal data to pursue individuals considered gay or gender-nonconforming, and it calls on the regime to end discrimination and violence against LGBTI people.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing documentation: trans and gay residents report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the 2021 takeover; security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in earlier rule.

Interview-based reports from residents in-country and abroad record physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations, with visibly transgender people facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight International's 26 January 2022 report (43 pages, 60 interviews with residents in-country and abroad) is the specific source base for those accounts of threats, assault, blackmail and wrongful-detention risk after the 15 August 2021 takeover; it describes no trans-prisoner placement practice at all.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

Unresolved or unverifiable: enforcement figures rest on 2022-23 interview-based reports and 2025-26 international flogging counts rather than the regime's own statistics; most accounts predate the 2024 Morality Law's implementation, so current on-the-ground practice is inferred rather than directly documented; no tourist entry pathway exists to test in practice.

Prison-housing axis: there is no evidence at all on birth-sex vs identity placement, trans special units, or solitary/segregation practice — the only prison-relevant finding is general wrongful-detention danger; that gap is treated as danger here, because a regime that criminalises same-sex conduct and abuses queer detainees cannot be assumed to place trans prisoners safely.

rewrites.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented at state level in Queensland: under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023) and its August 2023 inspection standards, transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender — identity-based placement — but staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process; the 2009 Corrective Services procedure this oversight replaced was assessed as largely ineffective. Placement practice in the other states is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context: the national legal trend is settled and protective — federal sex-discrimination protection (2013), the 2024 federal court reading of it, and rapid state modernisation — while the live policy pressure documented nationally is the organised exclusionary campaign landscape (facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures).

History and framing: state-by-state decriminalisation unfolded over decades from laws inherited from the historic metropole (one state kept the death penalty until 1949), and the national protections debate includes an ongoing terminological dispute over whether intersex people belong inside the same framework — framing, not visitor-facing risk. A federal hate-crime offence (2025) and conversion-therapy bans covering most of the population (2024) extend the protective layer beyond the earlier baseline.

Policy evolution behind the placement standard: the 2009 Queensland Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009), and oversight shifted to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 — institutional history rather than a visitor-facing risk.

State-level legal gender recognition remains a patchwork (only some jurisdictions are self-declaration) and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

rewrites.summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas. The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is a documented law-practice gap: under the National Council of Justice's Resolution 348 (13 Oct 2020, amended 2021) a person is recognised as LGBTI for custody purposes by self-declaration before a judge, the judge fixes the place of detention in a reasoned decision after consulting the person's preference, must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit and within it the general population or specific wings or cells, records the declared preference (with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat), and may not use LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation; yet the only state-level census in these sources — 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed inside eleven units treated as masculine across Rio de Janeiro state (April–June 2021) — found them housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement documented as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Dating-app robbery schemes (documented as fatal for gay men) are a caution for trans visitors using apps.

Custody framework context: the national placement framework (CNJ Resolution 348/2020, amended 2021) is judiciary-level machinery rather than a visitor-facing protection, and the census documenting birth-sex practice was produced with a lead author inside the LGBTI health division of Rio de Janeiro's state penitentiary administration — the gap between norm and practice is documented from inside the system.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The name/gender-marker change procedure and the transphobia criminalisation are resident-facing legal machinery; the world's-highest trans murder toll falls on local trans people, concentrated in poor and marginalised communities.

The custody practice is resident-facing: the Rio de Janeiro state census (138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed in eleven units treated as masculine, April–June 2021) documents travestis and trans women housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement framed as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations; state law has since 2015 granted them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics), and the national norms let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine — a visitor meets all of it only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Brazil's general crime problem (armed robbery, express kidnappings, gang violence) drives all governments to advise a high degree of caution for every traveller.

Prison axis: enforcement of the CNJ framework is documented only to the extent of the one Rio de Janeiro state census (2021); no source in this record tracks whether other states follow the Resolution's consultation and placement rules, and no data on solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners appears — the ban on using LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation is the norm on paper (Art. 11, VI–VII), not documented practice.

Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. rewrites.summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024). The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction, and there is no rollback movement.

The consequence axis of an arrest is only partly documented. Detention law is cantonal: the one explicit placement rule on record is Basel-Stadt's detention law (Justizvollzugsgesetz, adopted 13 November 2019), whose separation provisions require female and male detainees to be separated and stipulate that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate allowed to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No national placement rule, trans-prisoner case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented in any source in this record, so placement for a detained trans visitor is a cantonal question that is otherwise undocumented — and detention under a standard with no national guarantee and an explicit deviation power cannot be assumed to follow identity-based placement in every canton.

rewrites.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).

The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented: the only prison-axis source in this record — Human Rights Watch's Côte d'Ivoire country page — contains no document, case or report on transgender prisoners, nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary/segregation practice in Ivorian prisons. In a state with no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection and an inadequate police response to organised targeting, an undocumented placement practice cannot be read as a protected one: a detained trans visitor would be held in a prison system with no documented housing standard and no documented recourse.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Reputation and regional context: long considered the region's tolerant outlier, the country's standing is now in sharp downshift. A regional rights framework exists — a continental resolution marking a decade of advancing LGBT+ rights — though its protective operation here is not evidenced in this record.

rewrites.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as a policy-practice gap: since June 2017 the Justice Ministry has announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility — relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, with a census of self-identified trans prisoners ordered and an exclusive module for trans people under consideration. The practice side diverged: a June 2019 investigation found a trans woman serving a ~6-year sentence at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, where the prison offered only two options — 'you're a man or a woman here' — and she recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape at La Reforma (Alajuela) that a custodian witnessed; the Justice Ministry then counted 23 transgender people in the national system. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a formal identity-based choice policy whose documented practice still placed trans women in men's facilities in 2019, with violence and custodial inaction.

The 2017 placement policy was presented as modelled on Spain's system, with protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016 — institutional context for the choice policy rather than a visitor-facing protection.

rewrites.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented rather than hypothetical: in September 2018 a Salalah court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and publishing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video — the judicial outcome of the January 2018 police arrests under the Penal Code's Article 22, which penalises appearing in female clothing or demeanour. A gender-nonconforming visitor detected on arrival can therefore be jailed, and nothing in the sources records where inside the prison system such prisoners are held.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Comparisons with neighbours: sources note the explicit anti-trans statute is unusual in its region, and the traveller's public warning told others "do not go to these countries." The national enforcement pattern is active — the 2018 arrests were publicly announced after private-party photos circulated on social media, showing active monitoring of gender non-conformity.

The September 2018 sentences completed the documented enforcement loop: eight months after the January 2018 police arrests, the Salalah preliminary court convicted the four men under Article 22 of the July 2018 Penal Code — which allows up to one year's imprisonment and an OMR 3,000 fine for "any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor" — with the stiffer three- and four-year sentences carrying additional charges for publishing immoral acts on social media. Court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people is the recorded pattern, not an isolated event.

rewrites.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming. Even the custody consequence axis is comparatively benign: at a 2023 parliamentary hearing the National Rehabilitation Institute's director stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to go to a men's or women's prison, trans women are currently placed in women's prisons, and a dedicated trans sector was planned for a new Montevideo prison — though he conceded the gap: "the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line."

rewrites.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law. The lag is documented, with an improving record: in May 2018 the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after finding the authorities had "knowingly and repeatedly" held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers and suffered insults and "continuous sexual abuse and violence"; since the 2013 gender-law reform, trans and gender-diverse inmates transfer to the female section and now receive individual cells there, though a 2024 University of Malta study still records misgendering by officers and clothing and healthcare gaps.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux at the border: in July 2025 an international-court intervention was filed concerning an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in 2023 and facing a removal order — direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at the borders of the nation, though an asylum context rather than the ordinary visitor pass-through, and its outcome is pending.

The 2018 damages ruling is the prison-axis legal record: the civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded each of the seven women €4,000 for breach of rights and €1,000 for damage to personal dignity, ordered the director of prisons to pay, and the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the claimants — a binding judicial finding that prison authorities knowingly and repeatedly placed the inmates at high risk of sexual and psychological violence, with transfer to the female section refused in practice because it would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-determination legal gender recognition regime and passport 'X' markers are resident-facing administrative law; the prison healthcare and placement gaps concern resident inmates, with institutional practice found out of sync with national gender-identity law. A regional residents' survey ranks workers here top for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

The custody record concerns residents: the seven 2018 claimants stayed in the male section because transfer to the female section would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, while female inmates and warders were said to be hostile; current practice — transfer to the female section with individual cells, following earlier segregation in a separate dormitory (staff rationale: "the risks of pregnancies") — governs resident inmates, not visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.

rewrites.summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors: official WorldPride 2026 guidance confirms visas and entry depend only on nationality, not gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed at the border. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and since July 2025 a discriminatory motive is a statutory aggravating factor that can increase penalties by up to a third.

Practical safety supports are strong: Amsterdam operates dedicated reporting networks for LGBTQIA+ incidents, the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents for 2026, and the capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime. Same-sex marriage is legal and non-binary people are recognised, so a trans traveller's partner status raises no border or legal problems.

The genuine caution is rising reported hostility: discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people reached 4,800 last year, up 51% in a year for transgender-specific reports and 81% since 2022, and many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this chiefly means a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger. If a visitor is nonetheless detained, the custody consequence axis is a documented legal gap: no statute or regulation governs where transgender detainees are held — the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees — and the prison service places detainees by the gender designation in municipal records plus case-by-case factors (including the detainee's own preference), with transgender detainees frequently held on an "Extra Care Facility" wing alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders; courts have treated a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier, and a February 2024 human-rights lawyers' advisory called the unregulated placement "worrying and undesirable".
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National policy turbulence is pending rather than in force: a self-identification gender-recognition bill was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; neither currently changes the border or discrimination rules a visitor faces.

Comparative context: the nation ranks #13 on a comparative rights map and #2 of 121 regions as a "good place", with public support at 52%; at the same time there is no statutory definition of "hate crime" at national level, the police recording hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated expertise centre.

Custody-policy flux: the national human-rights lawyers' committee (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection in February 2024 that no law, regulation or official policy governs transgender detainees' placement; the prison service confirmed placement by municipal-record gender plus case-by-case factors, the custodial-institutions agency said it was drafting guidelines that remained unpublished as of the sources, and the advisory urged rules aligned with Council of Europe CPT standards — policy in motion rather than in force.
rewrites.localsOnly:

rewrites.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

Officials also cite the fear of people accused of sex offences ‘identifying as transgender’ to enter female housing with born-male offenders as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.

rewrites.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

The consequence axis of an arrest is directly documented. A 2018 academic study of Jamaican prisons — estimating that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities — reported that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender ‘are isolated’, that rehabilitation opportunities are ‘basically non-existent’, that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent ‘corrective rape’. The US State Department’s 2023 report confirms the state dimension: ‘prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity’, in facilities so overcrowded that Tower Street maximum-security cells held three times capacity, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. Jamaica bars legal gender registration, no specialised trans housing policy is documented, and for a detained trans visitor this is identity-targeted violence on top of an already severe, overcrowded baseline — a documented tier of its own, not merely an elevated version of a general prison risk.

rewrites.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT “propaganda” law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through a single contested case: a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007) served his sentence at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, where he says he was held alone in unsanitary cells — three years fully isolated from other detainees per a 2025 corroboration — including long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the ward for detainees requiring protection) was refused and no special-unit option existed. He described staff humiliation (forced strip body searches, demeaning roll-call name-calling, bathroom-door intrusion) and said only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The penitentiary administration contested the account, replying that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. For a visitor, the practical lesson is that a detained trans person in Moldova's system faced solitary-style isolation presented as protection, a refused protection-ward transfer, no special-unit option, and an administration that denies mistreatment — in a country that is otherwise the safest in its neighbourhood.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Context rather than visitor-facing mechanism: Moldova is on the EU accession path, which drives continued legal alignment. Legal flux: in 2013 an appeals court struck down a local “gay propaganda” ban as unconstitutional after church-led bans and protests against the anti-discrimination law; hate speech remains serious with no meaningful state response, and election-period political hate speech has risen, per the 2024 review. A recent travel feature portrays the country as slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity, with public Pride proceeding openly.

Custody-axis flux: the detainee said he would sue in Moldovan courts and the European Court of Human Rights, and the investigative outlet notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M — litigation and oversight-institution channels, not yet outcomes; the authorities publicly acknowledged that homophobia still persists in state institutions and announced staff training and stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment, an institutional acknowledgment with no enacted change on record.

rewrites.summary:
Luxembourg is exceptionally safe — among the strongest trans jurisdictions in its region. Legal gender recognition by self-determination has existed since 2018 (Act of 10 August 2018) with no medical requirements, and notably the process is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is banned across employment, goods, services, education, and health; a national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018; an equality body handles complaints.

No traveler-facing concerns exist: no bathroom laws, no border issues (entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans violence pattern. Gaps are minor: no nonbinary marker, and gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly covered in anti-discrimination law — a visitor-specific impact is not documented.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented as comparatively protective: per the Justice Minister's 2015 parliamentary answer, prison staff place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, trans-detainee situations are handled case by case, requests to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen form of address (a 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname); such cases are described as “exceptional”. No codified birth-sex placement rule, no trans special custody unit, and no solitary or administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners is documented, and the planned Uerschterhaff prison at Sanem was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation — so a visitor who ends up in custody is met by case-by-case accommodation under an explicit official warning against stigmatising or isolating LGBT detainees, not by a fixed rule.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Legal trajectory: the self-determination regime replaced a long, costly judicial procedure — a bill was presented in May 2017 and parliament approved the simplified civil-status change in July 2018. In July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ action plan, criticised by local organisations for missing depathologisation and other elements. A 2019 report noted the law lacked LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances while the justice minister signalled evolution after a monitoring body's intervention.

Custody-axis context: the only prison-axis documentation is the 2015 parliamentary answer — placement following disclosed identity/need case by case, an explicit ministerial warning against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate LGBT detainees, and the Justice Ministry's statement that no statistics on LGBT prisoners are kept because disclosure cannot be compelled without unlawful privacy interference.

Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented and grim: since the state of exception began (March 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in the mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. rewrites.summary:
South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

The consequence axis of an arrest is largely undocumented: no source in this record describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice — and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced. The one documented trans-in-state-placement case is military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty — a harsh institutional default corrected by the courts only after death. For a detained trans visitor, civilian-prison placement is simply unknown: in a legal system where legal gender recognition is possible and courts have repeatedly ruled for trans people, recourse would likely exist, but the placement practice itself is unverified — not a verified midpoint and not verified safe.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Compared with its closest comparable peers, the legal baseline has documented gaps: no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage. Policy and litigation flux: a December 2024 martial-law crisis and related assembly-freedom questions, a 2024 constitutional ruling recognising same-sex partners' healthcare rights, and organised conservative opposition set a moving political backdrop rather than direct street-level risk.

Custody-axis framing: the only trans-in-state-placement case on record is a military conscript case — Byun Hui-su's discharge, death, posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition — rather than a civilian prison case; the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel (Military Criminal Act article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment) and the exclusion of transgender people from military service are resident-conscript-facing, not visitor-facing.

rewrites.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist. Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is undocumented: the only prison-axis finding in this record — a Wikipedia survey of LGBTQ people in prison — contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in Mexico (no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice); its sole Mexico-specific item is a July 2007 Mexico City policy, adopted through the human-rights commission (CDHDF), allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. In a federation where legal gender recognition is state-by-state and official discrimination and near-total impunity for anti-trans violence are documented, where a detained trans visitor would be housed is unverifiable and cannot be assumed to follow identity.

rewrites.summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece. Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

The consequence axis of an arrest is a documented default-plus-petition system: placement of trans women detainees started from the registered sex — the four trans women transferred to Korydallou's women's prisons on 4 December 2021 had previously been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender — and a decision of that date by the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy created an on-request transfer route to women's facilities, the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in the country. No special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement are documented. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a registered-sex default with an on-request transfer route that demonstrably exists but runs through administrative petition — a workable-but-request-dependent outcome consistent with the country's law-versus-practice gap.

rewrites.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, released on 5 August 2024. rewrites.summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year. If a trans visitor is arrested or detained here, the custody consequence of the lagging framework is documented rather than theoretical: facilities house inmates by their family-register (registered) sex rather than gender identity — a women's prison in Gifu held an inmate registered female who identifies as a man, and a transgender activist was held among men for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention, initially denied hormone treatment, mocked for his identity during interrogations, and allowed to shower away from other detained men only after requests, with hormones arriving only after a doctor recommended them. Prefecture-level pressure over an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle went unresolved for years before a bar association issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time — a baseline for comparing how far institutional protection has moved.

Custody-policy flux surrounds the placement practice: the Gifu Prefecture Bar Association's September 2023 formal ‘warning’ to Kasamatsu Prison followed years with no policy change on an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle, and Human Rights Watch (June 2025) frames the pre-trial detention of a transgender activist — held among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it — within its broader “hostage justice” criticism of Japan's general pre-trial detention system, a burden every detainee faces that falls harder on a transgender detainee.

rewrites.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime. The gap extends into custody: because no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, placement follows legal sex in documented cases — a trans activist who became a detainee while protesting the junta in June 2015 was sent to a men's prison, told “she remains a man” and harassed during intake — while the Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, holds transgender inmates in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men at Pattaya Remand Prison, and accepts that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement. A trans visitor detained in Thailand therefore meets an unresolved placement practice: birth-sex men's facilities in documented cases, separated LGBT wings in others, with no guaranteed identity-matched housing.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.

Custody-policy flux: after reports of abuse and the documented placement of a trans woman in a men's prison in 2015, the Department of Corrections announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility — reported in 2016-17 as a possible world-first exclusively-LGBTQ prison — which activists welcomed while fearing it “could encourage exclusion” and insisting placement “should be an option, not an obligation”; department counts at the time recorded roughly 4,448 LGBT-identified people among about 300,000 prisoners (34 of them transgender), with a 2017 figure of more than 6,000 registered as sexual minorities.

rewrites.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub. The protections do not reliably reach custody: documentation shows Israel's response to transgender-prisoner vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at times been held in men's prisons — but courts have intervened case-by-case, most notably an October 2019 ruling that ordered the prison service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.

rewrites.summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while Davao City Jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested in the Philippines has no documented path to identity-matched custody.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
A national anti-discrimination equality bill has been stalled in the national legislature for 25 years, and no national legal gender recognition law exists; the 2025 killings are being cited by activists as an urgent reminder for the bill's passage. This is national legislation flux that may colour a visit, not a direct travel restriction.

Custody-policy flux: the documented official response is administrative segregation rather than gender-matched placement — the BJMP-Davao Community Relations chief said LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail are relocated in batches to the City Jail Annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment (March 2023); a Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism investigation (December 2022) documents that at Manila City Jail transgender women and gay men held in the ordinary male dormitories use informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates as a survival and protection strategy against abuse.

rewrites.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

The custody axis completes the picture: the state operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the state serve their time in Italian prisons with costs covered by the state, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.
